Thursday, 11.40 pm
Four nights in a row I was up past two playing online chess. Tonight I'm writing this instead, because today was bad.
Morning: skipped breakfast, too sleepy. Maths: Siddharth asked for my ruler and I said, "Buy your own," loudly, in front of everyone. He looked at me like I was a stranger.
Lab: Sir asked me to redo my readings and I said, "I don't care," and walked out. I have never done that. I got a note for Papa to sign. He'll say, 'What happened to my good boy?'
Evening: I felt low, like everything was pointless, and ate two packets of chips for dinner.
The weird part is I wasn't even angry at them. I was just tired and empty.
New rule, my own: phone goes in the kitchen at eleven. Proper dinner. Tomorrow I say sorry to Siddharth and to Sir.
Manoj

I'm Tarun. I run the tea stall outside the metro station in Hyderabad, and for most of last year, Anand was a regular.
He was a delivery rider, about twenty-four, always on his phone for orders. I found out slowly that he slept in a shared room with eight men and ate once a day, mostly my bun and chai. When the youth centre next door put up a poster for a free computer course, the other riders teased him: "Too lazy to fill a form?" He just shrugged and said, "Next month." Next month never came.
Then in spring a social worker from the centre helped him get a hostel bed and a meal card. Within weeks he looked different, less grey. One morning he borrowed my pen and filled that form, right here on my counter.
He wasn't lazy. He was just too tired and hungry to think past today.

qa.a: Right here on my counter, at Tarun's tea stall.

I'm Sharmila, Minakshi's cousin; we shared a room during her final year of nursing. In March the big hospital chain in Gurgaon offered her a job in their corporate wing: glass building, good salary, their name printed on everyone's lanyard. Our aunties were thrilled.

Then she applied to a rural health fellowship in Jharkhand, two years, a small stipend. She read the fellowship brochure the way other people read love letters.
The morning she declined the hospital job, her hands were shaking. She said, "I'm scared, Sharmila." But an hour later I found her humming and folding clothes, calmer than I'd seen her all year.
I don't know everything she weighed. But she seemed to fit her choice.

passage:
The ITI workshop in Belagavi closed at five, but Manjula, the senior instructor, kept noticing one bench still lit. Devika, nineteen, enrolled in the electrician course, had found three broken sewing machines in the store and was taking one apart, oil on her wrists, humming.
It was not in the syllabus. There were no marks for it. "Just want to see why the bobbin jams," Devika said, not looking up.
Manjula watched her for a week. Devika stayed late every day, and her notebook filled with drawings of gears.
When Devika's uncle visited and said she should drop all this and prepare for the bank exam, Manjula said nothing against him. She simply cleared a corner bench, labelled it with Devika's name, put a repair manual and a set of small screwdrivers on it, and said, "Use it when you want. Whatever you decide."

qa.q: What was Devika taking apart?
qa.a: One of three broken sewing machines from the store.

qa.q: What does Devika's humming and staying late suggest she feels about the work?
qa.a: It suggests she finds real joy and curiosity in fixing the machines for their own sake, since there are no marks for it.

qa.q: Which of Manjula's choices supported Devika best, and why?
qa.a: Clearing a bench with her name, a manual and screwdrivers gave Devika tools and space, while 'Whatever you decide' left the career choice to her.

qa.q: How might Devika's uncle see her late evenings at the workshop?
qa.a: He may see them as a distraction from the bank exam, not realising how much the work lights her up.

grounding: It shows a mentor noticing a young woman light up and stay late over work that carries no marks, and giving her space and tools without pressing a set career.
